newsitem.title: CANADA: Air Canada still seeks ValuJet deal.
newsitem.headline: Air Canada still seeks ValuJet deal.

text.p: Air Canada president and chief executive officer Lamar Durrett said on Tuesday that the airline remains interested in obtaining a contract for the maintenance of ValuJet Inc's DC-9 aircraft.
"We are interested in that contract," Durrett told reporters after a luncheon speech.
He said Air Canada had had recent discussions with Atlanta-based ValuJet regarding the maintenance contract but that no announcement was imminent.

In his speech, Durrett said Air Canada would be adding more employees at its third-party maintenance facilities in Montreal. The carrier had laid off about 500 workers earlier this year after a Northwest Airlines contract ended.
After his speech, Durrett said Air Canada plan to add about 60 new jobs at its aircraft engine repair operations in Montreal.
On ongoing labor contract talks at Air Canada, Durrett said he was optimistic the carrier would work out its differences with its regional pilots and about 3,500 sales and service agents.
"As long as people are talking, we are going to remain optimistic that we're going to be able to work out any differences through the due course of the negotiation process," Durrett said.

Earlier this month, members of the Canadian Auto Workers union local 2213 representing 3,500 sales and service agents voted in favor of strike action if talks fail. The union said the workers could be strike ready for the Christmas season.
"Clearly, if something were to happen where we had a strike or work stoppage, it would not be a positive thing for the airline," Durrett said.

With ValuJet certified to fly again in the United States, the airline plans by the end of first-quarter 1997 to add 15 DC-9s to the 15 it is currently flying as it gradually brings its flight schedule back up to full strength, Durrett said.

ValuJet was grounded in June following the May 11 crash of one of its DC-9s in the Florida everglades, killing all 110 people on baord. Before the grounding, Air Canada had discussed maintaining the Atlanta-based carrier's DC-9 fleet at its facilities in Montreal. In late September, U.S. regulators allowed ValuJet to return to the skies, and discussions on the maintenance contract have resumed, he said.
Air Canada is also in contract talks with pilots at four of its five regional airlines serving the Canadian market.

Durrett said that he fully expects to see continued competition in the Canadian domestic market, particularly in the busy Montreal-Toronto-Ottawa triangle, from Canadian Airlines Corp, even if that airline consolidates somewhat in the coming months.

Durrett said competition in the domestic market has been brisk, given the arrival of carriers WestJet Airlines Ltd and Greyhound Air service. He does not expect a fast rise in U.S.-based airline activity in Canada soon, Durrett said.

Durrett noted Air Canada's first and second-quarter domestic yields were under pressure from the new competition, but he declined to comment on third-quarter results, which were scheduled to be released Wednesday morning.
Durrett said Air Canada is seeing renewed interest in its fleet of 35 DC-9 aircraft, which it is retiring, except for about 15, over the next few months.
On the topic of new routes to Asia, Air Canada would like to have daily flights from Vancouver to Hong Kong, instead of the four flights a week it has currently.
"Air Canada is ready with the airplanes, the personnel and the desire. We would like to go daily out of Vancouver and daily out of Toronto tomorrow," he said.
